meta.title: Who really said "It is only with the heart that one can see rightly; what is essential is invisible to the eye"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Verified: the fox says it in chapter 21 of Saint-Exupéry's The Little Prince (1943). But the famous English wording belongs to translator Katherine Woods.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It is only with the heart that one can see rightly; what is essential is invisible to the eye'?
meta.ogDescription: Real quote, real book, right author — chapter 21 of The Little Prince (1943). The catch: Saint-Exupéry wrote it in French. This sentence is Katherine Woods's.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1900–1944 · French aviator & author of Le Petit Prince
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and easy to place: it is the fox’s parting secret in chapter XXI of The Little Prince, published in New York in April 1943. One caveat worth knowing — Saint-Exupéry wrote it in French (“on ne voit bien qu’avec le cœur. L’essentiel est invisible pour les yeux”); this exact English sentence is Katherine Woods’s 1943 translation.

source.excerpt: “And now here is my secret, a very simple secret: It is only with the heart that one can see rightly; what is essential is invisible to the eye.”
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ places the line in chapter XXI and gives the French original alongside this exact English wording, plus four competing variant translations.

The CJV Lang survey of the fox’s secret dates “What is essential is invisible to the eye” to Katherine Woods (1943) ↗ and contrasts it with Richard Howard’s 2000 “Anything essential is invisible to the eyes.”
Wikipedia ↗ confirms the first edition: Reynal & Hitchcock, New York, April 1943, English and French together, with Woods (1886–1968) as the first English translator.
The Morgan Library’s catalogue record ↗ documents the surviving working manuscript, drafted c. July–October 1942 on onionskin paper and acquired by the Morgan in 1968.
source.excerptNote: Spoken by the fox as the little prince prepares to leave him, at the close of chapter XXI. Saint-Exupéry’s French reads: “Voici mon secret. Il est très simple: on ne voit bien qu’avec le cœur. L’essentiel est invisible pour les yeux.”

source.rightsNote: The Little Prince was first published in 1943, which puts it firmly under US copyright: it does not enter the American public domain until 2039 ↗, 95 years from first publication. Two layers apply here — Saint-Exupéry’s French text and Katherine Woods’s 1943 English translation, which is the wording quoted on this page. In France the term runs to 2033, extended by a wartime allowance and a further 30 years because Saint-Exupéry was declared “Mort pour la France.”

author.name: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
author.heading: The pilot who wrote the fox
author.bio: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry flew mail routes over the Sahara and the Andes before turning the experience into literature — Night Flight, Wind, Sand and Stars, and finally The Little Prince, which he wrote and illustrated during a wartime exile in New York and on Long Island in 1942. He was a working pilot to the end: in July 1944 he took off from Corsica on a reconnaissance flight and never came back, and France later designated him “Mort pour la France.” He never saw the book become one of the most translated works ever published.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: This one is not a fake — it is a rare case where a hugely popular quote is exactly what it claims to be. The errors here are subtler: who wrote the English, who says the line, and which translation you are actually holding.

items.why: Saint-Exupéry wrote “L’essentiel est invisible pour les yeux.” The sentence quoted on a million graduation cards — “what is essential is invisible to the eye” — is Katherine Woods’s 1943 rendering ↗. She chose the singular “eye,” and the rhythm that made it stick, and almost nobody credits her.

items.who: The fox, not the little prince
items.why: It is the fox’s parting secret in chapter XXI ↗, given to the prince as he leaves. It is routinely posted as though the prince, or Saint-Exupéry in his own voice, said it.

If you buy a new US copy, you will probably not find this line in it. Howard’s translation — the standard since 2000 — reads “Anything essential is invisible to the eyes” ↗. The Woods version was the English standard for decades before going out of print in 2000 ↗.

Keller’s similar-sounding line about the best and most beautiful things being “felt with the heart” gets swapped for this one and vice versa. It is a separate quote, and Quote Investigator traces it back to Keller’s teacher Anne Sullivan, via an 1891 letter ↗ — not to Saint-Exupéry.

misattribution.truthLine: Saint-Exupéry really wrote it, the fox really says it, and it is really in chapter XXI ↗. The English sentence you love, though, was written by Katherine Woods in 1943.

context.heading: Why the fox says it
lead: The fox has just taught the little prince what it means to tame something — that a rose becomes irreplaceable not because of anything visible about it, but because of the hours you poured into it. The secret is the fox’s goodbye gift: a rule for seeing that the prince needs in order to understand why his rose, an ordinary rose among thousands, is the only one in the universe.

It reads as gentle children’s-book philosophy, and it was written by a man in exile in wartime New York in 1942, drafting on onionskin paper, who would be flying reconnaissance missions over occupied Europe within two years. The tenderness is not naive. It was written by someone who knew exactly what was about to be invisible to him.
context.detailsSummary: How the book came to be written in New York
detailsBody: Saint-Exupéry drafted Le Petit Prince around July–October 1942 in Manhattan and on Long Island. The surviving working manuscript — 175 unbound onionskin leaves in pencil and ink, plus preparatory watercolours — is at the Morgan Library & Museum ↗, which purchased it in 1968. He had given it to a friend, Silvia, before leaving to rejoin the war.

Reynal & Hitchcock issued the English and French editions in New York in April 1943. The book did not appear in France until after the Liberation — Saint-Exupéry’s work had been banned under the Vichy regime.
context.pull: The fox is not telling the prince to feel more. He is telling him that what he already spent is what makes the rose real.
